module_name: Hitler's Experience in World War I

extracted_notes.text: In August 1914, at the outbreak of World War I, Hitler was living in Munich and voluntarily enlisted in the Bavarian Army.

Posted to the Bavarian Reserve Infantry Regiment 16 (1st Company of the List Regiment), he served as a dispatch runner on the Western Front in France and Belgium, spending nearly half his time at the regimental headquarters in Fournes-en-Weppes, well behind the front lines.
In 1914, he was present at the First Battle of Ypres and in that year was decorated for bravery, receiving the Iron Cross, Second Class.
During the war, he was saved by his commanding officer, Fritz Wiedemann, who pulled Hitler out of the rubble of a collapsed building while under heavy fire.
During the Battle of the Somme in October 1916, he was wounded in the left thigh when a shell exploded in the dispatch runners' dugout.
Hitler spent almost two months recovering in hospital at Beelitz, returning to his regiment on 5 March 1917.
He was present at the Battle of Arras of 1917 and the Battle of Passchendaele.
He received the black Wound Badge on 18 May 1918.

Three months later, in August 1918, on a recommendation by Lieutenant Hugo Gutmann, his Jewish superior, Hitler received the Iron Cross, First Class, a decoration rarely awarded at Hitler's Gefreiter rank.
On 15 October 1918, he was temporarily blinded in a mustard gas attack and was hospitalised in Pasewalk.
While there, Hitler learned of Germany's defeat, and, by his own account, suffered a second bout of blindness after receiving this news.

Like other German nationalists, he believed the Dolchstosslegende (stab-in-the-back myth), which claimed that the German army, "undefeated in the field", had been "stabbed in the back" on the home front by civilian leaders, Jews, Marxists, and those who signed the armistice that ended the fighting--later dubbed the "November criminals".
The Treaty of Versailles stipulated that Germany had to relinquish several of its territories and demilitarise the Rhineland.
The treaty imposed economic sanctions and levied heavy reparations on the country.
They especially objected to Article 231, which they interpreted as declaring Germany responsible for the war.

true_false_games.feedback: Incorrect. The myth claimed the army was undefeated in the field but was betrayed on the home front by Jews, Marxists, and civilian leaders.

true_false_games.statement: According to the 'stab-in-the-back myth', the 'November criminals' were the individuals who signed the armistice.
true_false_games.feedback: Correct. The 'November criminals' included those who signed the armistice, as well as Jews, Marxists, and civilian leaders.

true_false_games.statement: The Treaty of Versailles was viewed by many Germans as a 'Diktat' because it imposed harsh conditions and assigned guilt to Germany via Article 231.
true_false_games.feedback: Correct. Article 231 was interpreted as declaring Germany responsible for the war, contributing to the perception of the treaty as a forced peace.

true_false_games.statement: Adolf Hitler's enlistment in the Bavarian Army occurred after he was deemed unfit for service in the Austro-Hungarian Army.
true_false_games.feedback: Hitler was first deemed unfit for service by the Austro-Hungarian Army before voluntarily enlisting in the Bavarian Army in August 1914.

true_false_games.statement: Hitler was awarded the Iron Cross, First Class, before he received the black Wound Badge.
true_false_games.feedback: Hitler received the black Wound Badge on 18 May 1918, and the Iron Cross, First Class, later in August 1918.

true_false_games.statement: The mustard gas attack that temporarily blinded Hitler occurred prior to his hospitalization in Pasewalk.
true_false_games.feedback: The gas attack on 15 October 1918 led directly to his evacuation and hospitalization in Pasewalk.

true_false_games.statement: Hitler learned of Germany's defeat while he was serving as a dispatch runner at the regimental headquarters in Fournes-en-Weppes.
true_false_games.feedback: Hitler learned of Germany's defeat while hospitalized in Pasewalk, not at the headquarters in Fournes-en-Weppes.

true_false_games.statement: The recommendation for Hitler's Iron Cross, First Class, was made by Lieutenant Hugo Gutmann in August 1918, following Hitler's service in the Battle of the Somme.
true_false_games.feedback: While he served in the Somme, the Iron Cross, First Class, was awarded in August 1918 based on Gutmann's recommendation, long after the October 1916 Battle of the Somme.

true_false_games.statement: Hitler's participation in the First Battle of Ypres in 1914 preceded his involvement in the Battle of Arras and the Battle of Passchendaele.
true_false_games.feedback: The First Battle of Ypres occurred in 1914, while Arras and Passchendaele took place later in the war (Arras in 1917).

true_false_games.statement: The 'stab-in-the-back myth' (Dolchstosslegende) was embraced by Hitler after he had already been formally notified of the terms of the Treaty of Versailles.
true_false_games.feedback: Hitler embraced the myth in the vacuum of defeat following the capitulation in November 1918, which provided the fuel for his rhetoric when the formal peace terms were later announced.
